name: Effort Justification
description: After paying a meaningful effort cost to get something, people can value it more highly than the thing itself objectively warrants. Effort gets retrospectively rationalized into value.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to onboarding/setup friction, application funnels, premium unlocks, community initiation rituals, and customization flows: effortful entry can increase attachment or perceived value, but it can also be mistaken for genuine product quality.
myth_risk_note: Existing corpus backing is 'partial' because the directly verified classic evidence (Aronson & Mills 1959) is a narrow severe-initiation form; broader popular extensions to sunk-cost effects and the IKEA effect are related but mechanistically distinct -- Marsh, Kanngiesser & Hood (2017) even found effort does NOT moderate the IKEA effect in young children, suggesting the two phenomena diverge more than the shared 'effort justification' label implies.
prevalence_note: Recognizable in behavioral-design, gamification, community, and habit-formation conversations, but the exact label is used less often in day-to-day product discourse than sunk cost, IKEA effect, or loss aversion.

findings.description: Participants who endured a severe embarrassing initiation later rated the very same dull group discussion more favorably than participants who underwent a mild or no initiation. This classic severe-initiation result is the canonical early evidence for effort justification within cognitive-dissonance theory.
findings.source_title: The effect of severity of initiation on liking for a group.
findings.source_venue: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
